P0C82.d: P0C82 is the plausibility test for sensor H: its circuit is fine, but the temperature it reports strays too far from what the rest of the pack says. On the 2016 Cadillac ELR (16OBDG01) GM fails it when the reading differs from the average of the other module groups by more than 20 °C in 50 of 67 samples, Type B; the 2019 table 19OBDG02 allows 25 °C, sampled every 25 ms and only while no low, high or communication fau
s: Check-engine or hybrid lamp, often after the car has stood for a while
Battery power limited
c: Thermistor H reading off while still electrically valid
Sensor H lifted off its module, measuring air instead of cells
Genuine local temperature difference from poor coolant flow

P0C83.d: P0C83 stands for a sensor H voltage under its permitted range, which with an NTC thermistor reads as heat: a short to ground or a shorted element makes the cell group seem far too hot. GM's 2016 Cadillac ELR table (16OBDG01) fails it above 87.5 °C, an ADC count below 680, for 1.4 s in a 2 s window, two trips; the Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 files it as the low-voltage fault of sensor 8.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and strong power reduction
Live data shows sensor H far hotter than its neighbours
Battery cooling running at full effort
c: Sensor H signal shorted to ground or to the pack housing
Fault in the cell monitoring unit that reads sensor H

P0C84.d: P0C84 is set when the sensor H line sits too high in voltage, which the controller converts into an impossible cold reading. The pull-up drives an interrupted circuit upward, so an open wire, a pushed-out pin or a broken thermistor are the classic triggers.
s: Battery-too-cold message in mild weather
Electric drive limited or unavailable
c: Broken wire or backed-out pin in the sensor H circuit
False set by battery module software (GM Volt, 18-NA-342)

P0C85.d: P0C85 points to a sensor H reading that flickers. A battery pack warms and cools slowly, so fast swings in one channel suggest an electrical contact problem rather than real heat.
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Sensor H value jumping in live data
c: Intermittent contact at the sensor H terminal
Partly broken sensor H wire inside the pack harness
Noisy measuring channel on the sensing board

P0C86.d: P0C86 compares the neighbouring battery temperature sensors F and G with each other. After the pack has rested, both should settle to nearly the same value; a persistent gap means at least one reads wrong although neither circuit is open or shorted.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Somewhat reduced battery power
Sensors F and G far apart in live data after a cold soak
c: Thermistor F or G drifted without an electrical fault
Sensor F or G no longer in contact with its module
Real temperature difference between the two module groups
Battery management calibration with an overly narrow window

P0C87.d: P0C87 checks that battery temperature sensors G and H tell a consistent story. The controller would set it when, after enough rest for the pack to equalise, the two values remain apart by more than a calibrated margin.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Reduced charge and discharge power
c: Thermistor G or H drifted while staying in range
Sensor G or H detached from its cell group
Real temperature gap from a weak cell group or blocked cooling
Battery module software needing an update

P0C88.d: P0C88 is the general circuit code for battery temperature sensor I, chosen when the fault is electrical but not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P0C88 publicly.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Reduced electric power
Generic scan tools may show the code without a description
c: Connector fault on the sensor I circuit
Defective input channel in the battery sensing electronics

P0C89.d: P0C89 says sensor I delivers an electrically valid but implausible temperature. GM checks it against the average of the remaining sensors: the 2019 table 19OBDG02 fails it beyond 25 °C in 50 of 67 samples, Type B, two trips, and suspends the test while a low, high or communication fault is present; the 2016 Cadillac ELR table (16OBDG01) uses 20 °C.
s: Check-engine or hybrid lamp, often after a long rest
Battery power reduced
c: Module software setting the code falsely, fixed by reprogramming (GM Volt)
Thermistor I drifted within its electrical range
Sensor I displaced from its measuring point
Real local heating at the cell group of sensor I

P0C8A.d: P0C8A records a sensor I voltage below the valid band. As the element is an NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up, a low voltage translates into a cell group that seems dangerously hot, typically caused by a short to ground.
s: Warning lamp with reduced power
Sensor I shown extremely hot in live data
Battery cooling running continuously
c: Sensor I signal shorted to ground
Thermistor I shorted, for example after coolant or moisture entry
Cell monitoring unit input for sensor I faulty

P0C8B.d: P0C8B covers a sensor I signal stuck above its valid voltage, which the controller interprets as extreme cold. An interrupted circuit lets the pull-up lift the line, so the root cause is usually an open connection or a failed thermistor rather than the weather.
s: Battery-too-cold message although outside temperature is mild
Electric drive limited or unavailable
Battery heater running unnecessarily
c: Open wire or loose connector in the sensor I circuit
Battery module software causing false cold readings (GM Volt, 18-NA-342)

P0C8C.d: P0C8C reports that sensor I changes faster and more often than any real battery temperature could. GM is the only maker that publishes the test: in 19OBDG02, the 2019 hybrid powertrain control module 2 table, each 10-sample window at 100 ms per sample is scored by the summed absolute change of the reading, a score above 10 counts as a failed window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 set the code, Type B, two trips, with
s: Warning lamp appearing now and then
Sensor I value jumping in live data
Short phases of reduced power
c: Fretting or loose terminal on the sensor I connector
Sensor I wire broken inside its insulation
Sensing board with unstable supply or ground

P0C8D.d: P0C8D covers electrical trouble in the circuit of battery temperature sensor J that the controller cannot pin down to a low, high or jumping signal. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P0C8D.
s: Hybrid system warning, on many models also the check-engine lamp
Less electric power and slower charging
c: Corroded or loose plug between sensor J and the monitoring board
Faulty input channel on the cell monitoring board

P0C8E.d: P0C8E sets when sensor J delivers an electrically valid temperature that disagrees with the other modules. For the 2012 Volt, table 12OBDG01A runs the check only after propulsion, off-board charging and battery conditioning have all been inactive for more than 21,600 s, so the pack should be evenly soaked; a gap above 25.3 °C to the mean of the remaining sensors in 50 of 67 samples fails it, Type B.
s: Warning lamp appearing after the car has been parked for many hours
Battery power reduced while the pack is cold or warm
c: Thermistor J drifted but still within its electrical range
Sensor J no longer pressed against its cell group
Actual temperature difference from a weak cell or blocked cooling path

P0C8F.d: P0C8F means the voltage on sensor J has dropped below its valid window. The NTC thermistor is powered via a pull-up resistor, so a grounded signal line reads as an absurdly hot cell group; low refers to the signal.
s: Warning lamp with clearly reduced electric power
Battery fan or chiller running constantly
Engine starts more often on plug-in hybrids
c: Sensor J signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Thermistor J shorted internally, for example after moisture
Monitoring board input pulling the line low

P0C90.d: P0C90 reports the opposite case: sensor J reads above its voltage window, which with a pull-up circuit points to an open thermistor, a broken lead or a disconnected plug, and the controller sees an impossibly cold module. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02) a converted value colder than −69 °C in 8 out of 10 readings, one every 100 ms, fails the test; it is Type B, so the lamp waits for the second bad t
s: Battery-too-cold message although the weather is mild
Little or no electric drive power
Battery heater switching on without need
c: Open lead or unplugged connector at sensor J
Terminal pushed back in the monitoring board plug

P0C91.d: P0C91 watches for a sensor J reading that changes too fast and too often for a heavy battery. GM's tables 16OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 add up how far the value moves between samples over a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failing windows out of 5, about half a second, store the code, Type B over two trips.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes between drives
Sensor J value jumping in live data
c: Fretting or loose terminal in the sensor J plug
Conductor broken inside the insulation, opening under vibration
Unstable reference or ground on the monitoring board

P0C92.d: P0C92 is stored when the input from battery temperature sensor K has an electrical fault that the controller leaves unclassified. Public manufacturer documentation for exactly this code does not exist.
s: Hybrid or EV warning message
Reduced electric power until the fault is repaired
c: Poor contact at the sensor K plug
Defective input channel on the cell monitoring board

P0C93.d: P0C93 compares sensor K with its neighbours: the reading is electrically fine but too far from the pack average. GM's 2016 hybrid table 16OBDG02 sets it when the absolute difference exceeds 25.00 °C for 50 samples out of 67 taken every 25 ms, roughly 1.7 s, rated Type B; the check is suspended whenever a low, high or erratic code for the battery sensors is active.
s: Warning lamp, often first noticed after a cold start
Charging and discharging power limited
c: Thermistor K reading off while still electrically valid
Sensor K lifted off its cell group
Real temperature spread from uneven coolant flow or a weak cell

P0C94.d: With P0C94 the controller sees the sensor K signal pulled below its lower limit, a pattern produced by a chafed wire touching ground or an internally shorted thermistor, which the conversion turns into an extreme temperature. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG02 counts a failure whenever the converted value is hotter than 160 °C and needs 8 such readings out of 10, one every 100 ms, Type B; in the 2012 Volt table the same sensor
s: Warning lamp and reduced electric power
Battery cooling running although the pack is not hot
c: Sensor K signal line shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant reaching the sensor K connection

P0C95.d: P0C95 is set when sensor K delivers a voltage above its valid range. In the usual NTC layout a broken circuit allows the bias resistor to drive the input high, so the controller sees an impossibly cold module.
s: Battery-too-cold or plug-in-to-warm message in mild weather
Electric power reduced or unavailable
c: Open circuit or disconnected plug at sensor K
Sensor lead damaged during earlier work on the pack

P0C96.d: P0C96 flags an unsteady sensor K signal, the kind of noise a loose contact produces while the value still sits inside its valid band. GM describes the monitor in 16OBDG02 and 18OBDG02: each 100 ms sample adds to a running total of absolute changes across 10 samples, a total above 10 marks the window as failed, and 4 failed windows in 5 store the code, Type B, so two bad trips are needed.
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Short spells of reduced power
c: Loose contact in the sensor K connector
Partly chafed sensor lead touching intermittently
Monitoring board with unstable supply or ground

P0C97.d: P0C97 is the catch-all for battery temperature sensor L, used when the input misbehaves electrically but fits none of the low, high or erratic categories. No manufacturer publishes this exact code.
s: Hybrid or EV warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Limited battery power
c: Connector fault between sensor L and the monitoring board
Faulty measuring channel on the monitoring board

P0C98.d: P0C98 is the plausibility code for sensor L: its reading is electrically valid but strays too far from the other sensors. GM's table for the 2012 Volt (12OBDG01A) runs the comparison only after more than 21,600 s with propulsion, off-board charging and thermal conditioning all off; a deviation over 25.3 °C, seen in 50 of 67 samples, counts as a Type B failure.
s: Warning lamp after a long standstill
Reduced battery power
c: Thermistor L drifted within its electrical range
Sensor L no longer in thermal contact with its cells
Genuine local temperature difference in that pack section

P0C99.d: P0C99 reports a sensor L voltage below the valid range. Because the thermistor works against a bias resistor on its monitoring board, any ground fault or an internally shorted sensor drags the voltage down, which reads as a very hot module.
s: Warning lamp and reduced battery power
Battery cooling running for no apparent reason
c: Sensor L signal shorted to ground
Monitoring board channel pulling the input low

P0C9A.d: P0C9A is the high-voltage fault of sensor L: an open thermistor, a broken lead or a disconnected plug lets the bias resistor raise the input, and the reading looks like deep frost. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG02 sets it when 8 readings out of 10, taken every 100 ms, are colder than −69 °C; it is Type B and requires more than 10.2 V supply plus working communication.
s: Battery-too-cold indication in mild conditions
Electric power reduced, engine running more on plug-ins
c: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor L
Corroded terminal with very high contact resistance

P0C9B.d: P0C9B covers a sensor L signal that jitters. GM's tables 18OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 integrate the absolute sample-to-sample changes over ten readings spaced 100 ms apart; when the integral exceeds 10, that window fails, and 4 failures within 5 windows store the code, classed Type B.
s: Warning lamp that may switch off again by itself
Erratic sensor L value in live data
c: Fretting pin in the sensor L connector
Cracked conductor in the sensor L lead
Loose ground on the cell monitoring board

P0C9C.d: P0C9C flags an electrical problem, not further classified, with current sensor B of the 14 volt power module, the DC/DC converter that supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the accessory power module (APM). In GM's 2013 eAssist table sensor B is the APM output current sensor, while sensor A (P0A86 to P0A8A) measures the input side.
s: Warning lamp, sometimes a charging-system message
12 V battery running low over time
c: Current sensor B inside the power module failed
Poor contact at the power module signal connector
Control software of the power module or hybrid controller

P0C9D.d: P0C9D means the output current reported by sensor B of the 14 V power module is electrically valid but implausible for the operating state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp without obvious driveability change
12 V battery charge state remaining low
c: Offset or gain drift of current sensor B
Converter output really differing from the commanded power
High resistance at the 12 V output cable or ground

P0C9E.d: P0C9E is set when current sensor B of the 14 V power module reads too little. GM documents it for the eAssist accessory power module in its 2013 table 13OBDG05C: the APM output current measured by the sensor must stay below 2 A for 1.5 s, counted as 60 of 80 samples at 25 ms, with the vehicle in run/crank; the code is Type B, so the MIL comes on after the second failing trip.
s: Check-engine lamp after two drives
Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights or warning messages
c: Output current sensor B failed inside the module
Sensor signal open or shorted to ground
Converter not delivering output although enabled

P0C9F.d: P0C9F reports an output current from sensor B of the 14 V power module that exceeds what the converter can plausibly supply. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C sets it once the APM output current reading tops 123 A while calculated APM input power is between 0.25 and 1.8 kW, supply voltage is 9 to 32 V and the vehicle is in run/crank; 1.5 s out of a 2 s window fail it, Type B, two trips.
s: Check-engine lamp
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery discharging
c: Internal defect of output current sensor B
Sensor signal shorted to a voltage source
Poor ground of the power module shifting the reading

P0CA0.d: P0CA0 covers short dropouts or spikes in the signal of current sensor B, the output-side sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter) in GM's numbering. Between the events the reading looks normal, which separates it from the hard low and high faults P0C9E and P0C9F.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional dim lights or voltage messages
c: Loose or fretting connector at the power module
Corroded ground or 12 V output connection
Current sensor B failing intermittently inside the module

P0CA1.d: P0CA1 is a request code, not a component fault: the drive motor control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine control module to light the MIL, which stores P0CA1. Subaru documents this on the 2014 XV Crosstrek Hybrid in bulletin 07-82-14R: P0CA1 sits in the engine module and C1424 in the stability control module, both MIL requests comparable to P0700.
s: Check-engine lamp, often with further warning lamps such as stability control
Hybrid drive behaving normally or with reduced electric assistance
c: Emissions-relevant fault stored in the drive motor control module
Module software reacting to a low 12 V battery (Subaru 07-82-14R)
Weak or discharged 12 V auxiliary battery

P0CA2.d: P0CA2 means the step-down function of the DC/DC converter, which brings high-voltage battery power down to the 12 V network, is not working correctly. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C uses it for a shoot-through fault inside the 14 volt power module: if the module detects a failed silicon power switch, a single 25 ms detection at 9 to 32 V sets the code as Type A, so the MIL lights on the first trip.
s: Check-engine lamp on the first trip, often with a charging warning
Falling 12 V voltage, low-voltage codes such as P0562
Hybrid assistance or auto-stop unavailable
c: Failed power semiconductor in the converter's step-down stage
Internal fault of the power module or power pack assembly
Spurious detection without a hardware fault, for example after supply dips

P0CA3.d: P0CA3 says the boost stage of a DC/DC converter fails to lift its output to the voltage the controller has requested. In full hybrids this stage, often called a boost or variable voltage converter, raises the traction battery voltage to a higher bus level that feeds the inverters.
s: Hybrid system warning with check-engine lamp
Noticeably reduced electric drive power or limp mode
Engine running more often than usual
c: Failed power transistor or driver in the boost stage
Internal fault of the inverter/converter assembly, e.g. reactor or capacitor
Wrong reading from the voltage sensor before or after the boost stage
Stored as a consequence of another hybrid system fault

P0CA4.d: P0CA4 is stored when the traction battery voltage climbs above its permitted limit while energy flows into the pack, for instance because a charger or the drive keeps pushing current although the cells are already full. Audi lists the code in TSB 2062631/5 from 2024 for the e-tron and Q8 e-tron family, there stored by the high-voltage charger module J1050 and described as an excessive battery load voltage.
s: Charging stops early or does not start
Code found during a check without any noticeable symptom
c: Charger or battery control software storing a false entry (Audi 2062631/5)
Charging current not reduced in time as the pack approaches full charge
Faulty pack or cell voltage measurement in the battery management

P0CA5.d: P0CA5 concerns a battery voltage judged too high while the pack is discharging, that is while it supplies the drive motor or other high-voltage consumers. Under load the terminal voltage normally sags, so an excessive value in this state points more to a measurement or plausibility fault than to genuine overcharge.
s: Hybrid or EV warning, often with check-engine lamp
Limited battery power output
c: Faulty pack voltage sensing in the battery management
Battery or hybrid control software evaluating the voltage wrongly
Loose or corroded high-voltage or sense connection

P0CA6.d: P0CA6 flags a current into the traction battery that exceeds what the control system expects. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV (2018 and 2022) stores it in the PHEV-ECU when, in charging mode, the measured battery current stays above the calculated charger output request for 5 s; suspects are the BMU, the onboard charger/DC-DC converter and the PHEV-ECU, and the repair is confirmed with drive cycle pattern 7.
s: Check-engine lamp, often found after charging
Charging interrupted or not possible
Vehicle not entering ready mode on some EVs
c: Onboard charger or DC-DC converter delivering more current than requested
Pack current sensor or battery management unit reading wrongly
Fault in the hybrid/PHEV control unit

P0CA7.d: P0CA7 is set when more current flows out of the hybrid or EV battery than the controller allows. Audi documents it on 48 V mild hybrids (A6, A7, A8, later also Q7, Q8 and S/RS versions, 2018 to 2024): the battery management of the 48 V battery, J1120, stores P0CA700 as discharge current too high, often with U046900 in the engine module, and the cluster shows an electrical system warning.
s: Electrical system or battery warning in the cluster
Start-stop or electric assistance temporarily unavailable
Check-engine lamp on plug-in hybrids
c: Starter/generator or battery module software (Audi 2058831, Stellantis 08-054-22)
Belt starter generator drawing excessive current
Battery current sensor or battery management misreading

P0CA8.d: P0CA8 is the general circuit code for battery temperature sensor M, meant for electrical faults that the controller does not sort into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer publishes this exact code.
s: Hybrid or EV warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Electric power reduced until repaired
c: Poor contact at the plug of sensor M on the monitoring board
Faulty input channel of the cell monitoring board

P0CA9.d: P0CA9 reports that sensor M stays within its electrical limits yet disagrees with what the remaining pack sensors measure. GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A only runs the comparison once drive system, plug-in charging and battery conditioning have rested for over 21,600 s; a spread above 25.3 °C from the mean in 50 of 67 samples is a Type B failure.
s: Warning lamp appearing after a long parking period
Battery power limited
c: Thermistor M drifting while staying in its electrical range
Sensor M lost thermal contact with its module
Module section genuinely warmer or colder, e.g. cooling fault or weak cell

P0CAA.d: P0CAA means the voltage at sensor M has dropped below its valid band. Sensor M is an NTC element supplied via a bias resistor on the board, so a grounded lead or a shorted element drags the voltage down and reads as an extremely hot spot.
s: Warning lamp with strongly reduced battery power
Battery cooling running without reason
c: Sensor M signal shorted to ground inside the pack
Measuring input of the cell monitoring unit defective

P0CAB.d: P0CAB is logged when the input of sensor M rises beyond its upper voltage limit. If the thermistor, one of its wires or the plug opens up, the pull-up resistor lifts the input, and the controller reads a temperature far below anything plausible.
s: Battery shown as very cold in mild weather
Reduced electric power, engine running more on plug-ins
c: Open circuit or unplugged connector of sensor M
Corroded or spread terminal at the monitoring board

P0CAC.d: P0CAC catches a sensor M signal that jumps around without necessarily leaving its permitted band. GM's HPC2 tables (16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02) add up the absolute changes between successive samples over a ten-sample window at 100 ms; whenever that total passes 10 the window is marked bad, and four bad windows in five lead to a Type B code after two trips.
s: Warning lamp that may go out again on its own
Jumping sensor M value in live data
c: Fretting or loose contact in the sensor M circuit
Cracked conductor or solder joint on the monitoring board
Unstable ground of the monitoring board

P0CAD.d: P0CAD stands for an electrical problem with battery temperature sensor N that the controller cannot assign to a specific failure type. Public manufacturer documentation for this exact code does not exist.
s: Hybrid or EV system message
Battery power reduced until repaired
c: Connector or wire fault between sensor N and the monitoring board
Faulty input channel of the cell monitoring board

P0CAE.d: P0CAE is the plausibility check for sensor N: the value is electrically acceptable, yet out of line with its neighbours. GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A demands a rest of more than 21,600 s without propulsion, external charging or thermal conditioning and then fails the test at a deviation above 25.3 °C in 50 of 67 samples, Type B.
s: Warning lamp after the car has stood for hours
Limited battery power
c: Thermistor N reading off while electrically valid
Sensor N detached from its cell or module surface
Real temperature difference in that pack section

P0CAF.d: P0CAF sets when the signal of sensor N is pulled under its lower voltage limit. A ground fault in the lead or a shorted thermistor causes this, and because the NTC sensor works against a pull-up resistor the controller interprets it as an implausibly hot module.
s: Warning lamp and markedly reduced battery power
Battery cooling running at full effort
c: Sensor N lead shorted to ground
Measuring input of the cell monitoring unit defective

P0CB0.d: P0CB0 reports a sensor N input above its upper voltage limit, which a pack controller reads as an unrealistically cold module. The NTC sensor is biased by a pull-up resistor, so any interruption in the element, its leads or its plug makes the input rise.
s: Battery reported as far too cold in mild conditions
Less electric range or power, engine starting more often
c: Open lead or disconnected plug of sensor N
Corroded terminal at the monitoring board

P0CB1.d: P0CB1 points to an unsteady sensor N signal rather than a lasting short or open. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG02 evaluates windows of ten samples, one every 100 ms, by integrating the absolute value of each change; above 10 the window counts as failed, and 4 failed windows within 5 set the code, Type B, two trips.
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Sensor N value jumping in live data
c: Loose or fretting pin in the sensor N circuit
Chafed or partly broken sensor N lead
Cracked track on the monitoring board

P0CB2.d: P0CB2 is the catch-all electrical code for battery temperature sensor O, reserved for circuit faults that are not classified as low, high or erratic. Publicly, no manufacturer documents this exact code.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Reduced electric power or charging rate
c: Poor contact at the sensor O connector on the monitoring board
Damaged lead between thermistor O and the board
Faulty measuring channel in the cell monitoring unit

P0CB3.d: P0CB3 is a plausibility code: sensor O delivers an electrically valid reading, yet it strays too far from the rest of the pack. In GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A the check waits until propulsion, plug-in charging and battery thermal conditioning have all been off for more than 21,600 s; a gap above 25.3 °C to the average in 50 of 67 samples then counts as a Type B failure.
s: Warning lamp typically appearing after the car has stood for hours
Battery power limited
c: Thermistor O drifting while its voltage stays in range
Sensor O no longer seated firmly against its module
Module section really warmer or colder, e.g. weak cell or uneven cooling

P0CB4.d: P0CB4 reports a signal voltage of sensor O below its lower limit. The sensor is an NTC thermistor biased by a resistor on the measuring board, so a short to ground or a shorted element looks like extreme heat.
s: Live data showing an implausibly hot module
Strongly reduced battery power with warning lamp
Battery cooling running without obvious need
c: Signal lead of sensor O shorted to ground in the pack
Input stage of the cell monitoring unit defective

P0CB5.d: P0CB5 is stored when the input of sensor O sits above its upper voltage limit. An open thermistor, a broken wire or a loose plug lets the pull-up resistor raise the input, so the controller sees a temperature colder than any real pack could be.
s: Pack shown as extremely cold regardless of weather
Less electric power, engine running more on plug-in hybrids
c: Open lead or unplugged connector of sensor O
Corroded or loose terminal at the sensing board

P0CB6.d: P0CB6 targets a sensor O signal that jitters or jumps instead of changing smoothly. Only GM's later HPC2 tables (16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02) define it: every 100 ms a sample is taken, the absolute steps between ten consecutive samples are summed, and a sum above 10 marks that window as failed.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Sensor O value jumping in live data
c: Fretting or loose terminal in the sensor O circuit
Cracked solder joint or trace on the sensing board
Chafed lead touching ground only under vibration

P0CB7.d: P0CB7 covers an electrical fault of battery temperature sensor P that the controller cannot pin down as low, high or intermittent. No manufacturer lists this code on a public official server.
s: Hybrid or EV warning message
Limited electric power until repaired
c: Loose or corroded plug of sensor P
Damaged wiring of sensor P inside the pack
Measuring channel for sensor P in the monitoring unit faulty

P0CB8.d: P0CB8 flags sensor P as implausible: its value is electrically fine, but after a long rest it disagrees with the temperature of the other modules. GM runs this comparison in the 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A only when drive system, external charging and battery conditioning have rested for over 21,600 s, so the whole pack should have settled; 50 of 67 samples more than 25.3 °C from the average give a Type B fault.
s: Warning appearing at the first drive after a long stand
Battery output restricted
c: Thermistor P drifted out of calibration
Sensor P detached from its module surface
Real temperature difference of that module, e.g. faulty cell

P0CB9.d: P0CB9 means the voltage of sensor P has fallen under the valid range. As with the other NTC sensors, low voltage corresponds to high temperature, so a short to ground or a collapsed thermistor makes the module appear to be glowing hot.
s: Module P shown as extremely hot in live data
Severe power limitation with warning lamp
c: Sensor P signal shorted to ground
Damaged input of the cell monitoring unit for sensor P

P0CBA.d: P0CBA appears when the signal of sensor P rises above its upper voltage limit, the typical picture of an open circuit: without a closed path through the thermistor, the pull-up resistor drives the input high and the computed temperature drops to an absurd value. GM's 2019 HPC2 table 19OBDG02 fails it when 8 of 10 readings at 100 ms fall below −69 °C, Type B, provided supply exceeds 10.2 V and the battery interface co
s: Very low battery temperature displayed on a warm day
Battery heater or engine running more than usual
c: Open circuit or disconnected plug of sensor P
Spread or corroded terminal on the sensing board

P0CBB.d: P0CBB is about short dropouts or spikes in the signal of sensor P that do not last long enough, or go far enough, to trip the low or high code. GM defines it in the HPC2 tables 16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02 and judges how restless the signal is: within each window of ten samples taken 100 ms apart the size of every change is added up, a total above 10 fails the window, and four bad windows in five produce the code, Type B, tw
s: Intermittent warning that may clear by itself
Erratic sensor P reading in live data
c: Intermittent contact at the sensor P plug
Hairline crack in the sensing board near the sensor P input
Unstable reference or ground of the monitoring unit

P0CBC.d: P0CBC is the general code for the sensor that measures coolant temperature in the cooling loop of drive motor A. Volvo and Polestar document it as P0CBC62 in the inverter module IEM of the Polestar 2 and the XC40/C40 Recharge (Technical Journals 37523 and 37521 from 2025): failure type 62 marks a signal comparison fault, and the vehicle displays a propulsion service message.
s: Propulsion system service message
Loss of drive power, car may stop on single-motor versions
Half power only on dual-motor versions
c: Faulty one-way valve in the drive unit coolant hose (Volvo/Polestar TJ 37521/37523)
Low coolant or trapped air in the drive motor loop
Sensor or wiring fault in the temperature circuit
Internal fault of the inverter module

P0CBD.d: P0CBD reports that the coolant temperature sensor of drive motor A gives a believable voltage but an implausible temperature. GM uses it on the 2013 eAssist models, where the drive motor is the belt-driven motor generator with its own small cooling loop.
s: Check-engine lamp after the second faulty trip
Reduced electric assist or regeneration
c: Coolant temperature sensor drifted out of its curve
Added resistance from a corroded connector
One of the comparison sensors (stator, intake air, transmission oil) reading wrongly

P0CBE.d: P0CBE says the coolant temperature input of drive motor A is below its valid range, meaning the sensor resistance has become very small. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C sets the code when the raw reading is under 100.9 Ω, which equals 120 °C, in 50 of 62 samples taken every 100 ms with the vehicle in run/crank; it is a Type B fault, so the lamp comes on after the second trip.
s: Check-engine lamp, possibly with ABS or brake assist warning
Hum or buzz from the right front
Electric assist restricted
c: Harness rubbing on crank or compressor pulley or belt (GM PIC5720A)
Loop genuinely very hot, e.g. pump or coolant fault

P0CBF.d: P0CBF is the code for an excessive signal from the coolant temperature sensor of drive motor A. With an NTC element a very high resistance stands for extreme cold, so in practice an open sensor, a broken wire or a disconnected plug is behind it.
s: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Coolant temperature of the motor shown at minimum value
c: Open signal or return wire, or unplugged sensor
Corroded pins at sensor or control module

P0CC0.d: P0CC0 is meant for a coolant temperature signal of drive motor A that drops out or jumps for short moments. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp that appears and disappears
Jumping coolant temperature value in live data
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed wire making contact only on bumps

P0CC1.d: P0CC1 concerns the control circuit of the electric pump that moves coolant through the loop of drive motor A, here specifically an open circuit. GM documents it for the 2013 eAssist hybrids, where the table 13OBDG05C calls the part the motor generator coolant pump: the output driver reports an open-circuit status, and 20 of 25 checks at 250 ms intervals with the vehicle in run/crank and the pump commanded off fail th
s: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Less electric assist and regeneration
c: Broken control or supply wire to the pump
Open winding inside the pump motor

P0CC2.d: P0CC2 judges whether the pump for drive motor A actually moves coolant, not only whether its wiring is intact. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C infers flow from temperature: when the model predicts more than 17 °C between the jacket coolant of the motor generator and the coolant reaching the loop sensor, a running pump should make the sensor warm up quickly.
s: Check-engine lamp
Electric assist reduced as the motor generator heats up
c: Air in the motor generator cooling loop, often after service
Low coolant level or kinked or blocked hose

P0CC3.d: P0CC3 indicates that the control line of the drive motor A coolant pump is pulled to ground. GM lists it for the 2013 eAssist cars in table 13OBDG05C: the hardware status of the output driver signals a low-circuit fault, and 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms with the pump commanded off and the vehicle in run/crank fail the test, Type B, so the MIL is lit after the second trip.
s: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Pump running constantly or not at all
Reduced electric assist
c: Faulty output stage in the control module

P0CC4.d: P0CC4 stands for a control line of the drive motor A coolant pump that is held at supply voltage or overloaded. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C the output driver reports a high-circuit status, and unlike the open and low checks this one runs while the pump is commanded on; 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms in run/crank set a Type B code, two trips.
s: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Pump silent when it should run
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying line
Water ingress in the pump connector

P0CC5.d: P0CC5 compares the two current sensors of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C, where the unit is the accessory power module (APM), sensor A measures the input and sensor B the output side.
s: Check-engine lamp after the second faulty trip
12 V battery not fully charged or low-voltage warning
c: Offset or gain drift of one current sensor
Internal fault of the power module, e.g. real efficiency loss
Calibration or software fault in the module

P0CC6.d: On plug-in vehicles the button that asks for the charge flap to open must also be able to rouse a sleeping control module, so it drives a separate wake-up line besides its normal signal. P0CC6 records that these two signals disagree.
s: Charge flap opens only after several presses or not at all
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Possible extra drain on the 12 V battery if the module is kept awake
c: Open, chafed or shorted wake-up wire between switch and control module
Worn or contaminated contact in the open request switch
Corroded or loose pins at the switch or module connector
Faulty wake-up input inside the control module

P0CC7.d: P0CC7 is the general circuit fault of the button that requests opening of charge flap A. GM reads this switch as a percentage of its reference and expects defined states; on the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt the code sets when the reading sits in a forbidden band between 65.9 and 81.6 percent, which indicates a wrong resistance, for instance a damaged switch or a partly broken wire.
s: Charge flap does not open with the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Opening via key, app or screen still possible on some models
c: Open request switch with wrong internal resistance
Partly broken wire or corroded connector raising circuit resistance
Faulty switch input in the control module

P0CC8.d: P0CC8 covers a plausibility fault of the charge flap A open request switch: the signal is electrically within limits, yet its behaviour makes no sense, for example a button that reports pressed for far too long or never changes state over many wake-ups. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Charge flap opens unexpectedly or ignores the button
Message about the charge flap in the instrument cluster
c: Mechanically sticking or jammed open request switch
Worn switch contact giving an implausible signal
Wiring fault that keeps the signal in an unexpected state

P0CC9.d: P0CC9 means the open request switch of charge flap A reads lower than any valid state, which typically results from the signal wire touching ground or from a switch that has failed short. In the Chevrolet Volt tables of 2011 to 2013, GM sets it once the reading drops under 22.9 percent of the reference in six of eight samples; the code is Type B, so the warning lamp follows after two consecutive trips.
s: Charge flap does not react to the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
c: Signal wire chafed through to body ground
Water in the switch connector creating a leakage path to ground

P0CCA.d: With P0CCA the control module sees the charge flap A open request switch signal above its highest valid level. Depending on the circuit, a wire shorted to battery voltage or an interrupted ground or switch path pushes the reading up.
s: Charge flap cannot be opened with the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
c: Signal wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Interrupted ground or switch return path
Pin pushed back in the connector

P0CCB.d: P0CCB flags a charge flap A open request switch whose signal jumps between states without a matching press, or drops out briefly. Such signals usually come from loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness that flexes with a door or body panel.
s: Charge flap opens only occasionally when the button is pressed
Fault comes and goes, often with temperature or road vibration
c: Loose or spread terminal at the switch or module connector
Cracked solder joint or worn contact inside the switch
Harness damaged where it flexes with a door or panel

P0CCC.d: The position sensor of charge flap A tells the vehicle whether the flap is open or shut; GM has patented a version in which a magnet on the flap acts on a magnetic sensor in the housing. P0CCC is the general circuit code for this sensor.
s: Flap-open message although the flap is closed
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Charging or charge pilot checks may be blocked
c: Faulty flap position sensor or switch
Sensor or its harness pigtail not fully seated in the housing
Damaged wire or corroded connector in the sensor circuit

P0CCD.d: P0CCD is set when the charge flap A position signal is electrically valid but does not fit what the flap should be doing, for example a state that disagrees with the last commanded movement. GM bulletin 25-NA-049 (March 2025) names the code for the Ultium models Cadillac Lyriq 2023 to 2025, Chevrolet Blazer EV and Equinox EV 2024 to 2025, and Cadillac Optiq and Escalade IQ 2025: drivers see a Service High Voltage mes
s: Service High Voltage message (GM Ultium models)
Flap status shown wrongly; another flap may be locked
c: Software anomaly in the battery control module (GM Ultium, bulletin 25-NA-049)
Position sensor giving a wrong end-position signal
Faulty harness between flap module and control unit
Flap not reaching its end position because of mechanical binding

P0CCE.d: P0CCE reports that the charge flap A position sensor signal has fallen below its lowest valid level, the classic sign of a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor that has failed short. GM documents it for the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt: the hybrid control module 2 sets it when the reading is under 22.9 percent of reference in six of eight samples, and as a Type B code the lamp comes on after two trips.
s: Wrong flap status in the display
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Charging may be refused
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Water in the flap area or sensor connector

P0CCF.d: P0CCF stands for a charge flap A position sensor signal above its highest valid level. A signal wire touching a 12 V feed, or an interrupted sensor ground that lets the input float upwards, are the usual explanations.
s: Flap status stuck or shown as open
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Interrupted sensor ground or open sensor

P0CD0.d: P0CD0 completes the position sensor group of charge flap A: the module sees the flap signal flicker or drop out for moments, without a lasting open, short or implausible state. Loose connector terminals, a sensor that is not held firmly in its seat, or a harness strained by the flap mechanism are the usual triggers.
s: Flap status in the display changes without reason
Sporadic charging or flap warnings
c: Loose terminal in the position sensor connector
Harness to the flap module chafed or under strain
Sensor or magnet not held firmly in its mounting

P0CD1.d: P0CD1 is the circuit fault of the output that releases charge flap A, normally a relay or driver that briefly powers the latch actuator. A GM patent shows such an actuator retracting a post so the spring-loaded flap can pop open.
s: Charge flap does not unlock
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Emergency release needed to reach the charge socket
c: Unlock actuator coil open or shorted
Faulty charge flap relay or its control wire
Chafed or corroded wiring to the actuator
Output driver in the control module damaged

P0CD2.d: P0CD2 is a functional test: after commanding charge flap A to unlock, the module waits for the position sensor to report the flap open. GM documents it for the Chevrolet Volt.
s: Flap does not open, especially in frost
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
c: Flap frozen, stuck to the seal or binding at the hinge
Weak or mechanically blocked unlock actuator
Misaligned charge port housing or hinge pin (GM PI0936)
Position sensor not registering the open flap

P0CD3.d: P0CD3 narrows the unlock output fault of charge flap A down to a low level: the monitored voltage on the actuator or relay control line stays near ground when it should be higher, which typically means a short to ground on the control wire or a failed actuator coil pulling the line down. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Charge flap does not unlock
Possibly blown fuse in the actuator supply
c: Actuator control wire shorted to ground
Shorted winding in the unlock actuator

P0CD4.d: P0CD4 is the high-level variant of the charge flap A unlock output fault. The control line reads high when the driver should be pulling it low or holding it off, as happens with a short to a 12 V wire, and on many low-side drivers also with an open actuator or broken wire.
s: Charge flap does not unlock or unlocks unexpectedly
Actuator may become hot from continuous current
c: Actuator control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Open actuator winding or broken wire
Output driver in the control module damaged

P0CD5.d: P0CD5 is the general circuit fault for the second coolant temperature sensor in the liquid loop of a hybrid or EV battery. In GM's tables for the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR, sensor B is the one at the pack outlet, an NTC thermistor read by the battery energy control module, while sensor A sits at the inlet.
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning lamp
Reduced charging or drive power, especially in heat or cold
Battery heating or cooling runs on substitute values
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector or damaged wire at the outlet sensor
Input circuit or reference in the battery control module faulty

P0CD6.d: P0CD6 means that coolant temperature sensor B at the battery outlet is electrically fine, yet its value does not fit the rest of the thermal system. GM runs the check in the hybrid controller of the Volt with the coolant pump above 20 % and no circuit faults present: if the outlet reading is more than 10 °C away from both the inlet reading and the mean cell temperature (2011 Volt, 80 of 100 samples at 100 ms), or at
s: MIL on, often without noticeable driving symptoms
Battery cooling or heating behaves unexpectedly
c: Outlet coolant temperature sensor reading off (drift)
Contact resistance at connector or terminals
Air or low coolant in the battery loop after service
Control module software sets the code incorrectly (e.g. Volvo XC90 T8)

P0CD7.d: P0CD7 reports that the signal of battery coolant temperature sensor B at the pack outlet has dropped toward ground. On an NTC thermistor with pull-up resistor a low voltage reads as very hot coolant, so a short to ground or a damaged sensor is the usual explanation rather than real overheating.
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Displayed outlet coolant temperature implausibly high
Charging or drive power reduced
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Sensor B internally shorted or water-damaged
Input stage of the battery control module faulty

P0CD8.d: P0CD8 is the high-voltage fault of battery coolant temperature sensor B at the pack outlet. On the usual NTC circuit the signal rises to the reference when the loop is broken, so the controller sees an impossible temperature below -40 °C.
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Outlet coolant temperature shows about -40 °C
Limited power or charging in cold weather
c: Connector of sensor B unplugged or not latched after service
Broken signal or ground wire, corroded terminals
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P0CD9.d: P0CD9 covers a signal from battery coolant temperature sensor B that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying inside the electrical limits most of the time. It is meant for loose terminals, chafed wires or a sensor that misbehaves only with vibration or temperature.
s: Check engine light, often after charging
Jumping outlet temperature value in live data
c: False detection after charging in warm weather (Volvo, software update)
Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor or module connector
Chafed harness that moves with the battery or body
Sensor B with an intermittent internal fault

P0CDA.d: P0CDA belongs to the rotor position sensor of drive motor A, normally a resolver: an excited stator winding induces signals in pick-up windings so the motor controller can work out rotor angle and speed. SAE counts the circuits of this sensor as A, B and C; GM, for instance, assigns circuit A to the S1/S3 winding and circuit B to S2/S4.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Electric drive limited or unavailable, engine runs more
Reduced regenerative braking
c: Loose, corroded or damaged resolver connector between motor and inverter
Resolver winding of circuit C defective
Evaluation circuit in the motor control module faulty

P0CDB.d: P0CDB flags circuit C of the drive motor A position sensor as present but implausible: its amplitude or phase, or the angle calculated from it, no longer agrees with the other circuits or with the observed motor speed. GM runs comparable tests on the main resolver signals, for example an amplitude check of the sine and cosine windings under P0A3F rated Type A, and limits for circuits A and B.
s: Hybrid system warning, MIL
Reduced electric power, engine starts in EV mode
Fault appears more often when the drivetrain is warm
c: Winding or terminal of the resolver changing its values when hot
Resolver shifted on its mount or rotor bearing play
Motor control module software or calibration

P0CDC.d: P0CDC reports that circuit C of the rotor position sensor on drive motor A reads below its permitted window. Typical reasons are a short to ground, a short between windings or a low-resistance path through moisture in the connector.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Electric drive limited, engine runs instead
Reduced or no regenerative braking
c: Circuit C wire shorted to ground or to another resolver wire
Moisture or corrosion in the resolver connector

P0CDD.d: P0CDD indicates that circuit C of the drive motor A position sensor reads above its limit, which in general points to an open winding, a disconnected plug or a short to a voltage source. Subaru uses the code in the drive motor control module of the 2014 XV Crosstrek Hybrid.
s: MIL on (requested via P0CA1 on Subaru)
Hybrid system warning, electric assist missing
c: 12 V auxiliary battery voltage dips with outdated module logic (Subaru)
Open winding, broken wire or disconnected resolver plug
Circuit C wire shorted to a voltage source

P0CDE.d: P0CDE describes a circuit C signal from the drive motor A position sensor that drops out or jumps briefly instead of failing for good. That pattern suits loose terminals at the resolver plug, a harness strained by drivetrain movement, or a winding or contact that opens only when hot.
s: Occasional jolt or hybrid system warning
Temporary switch to engine operation
Fault disappears after restart
c: Loose or spread terminal in the resolver connector
Harness strained or chafed by drivetrain movement
Resolver winding or joint that opens when hot

P0CDF.d: P0CDF signals an electrical fault in the drive circuit of coolant control valve A, the valve that routes or shuts off coolant to the hybrid or EV battery. Mercedes-Benz uses it in the battery management unit N82/2 of the S-, E- and C-Class hybrids, where it marks the actuation of the battery module coolant shutoff valve as electrically faulty or interrupted (service information LI83.30-P-061224, together with the stu
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Battery cooling or heating not working as intended
Reduced charging or drive power
c: Valve coil or actuator motor open
Broken wire or corroded connector at the valve
Driver stage in the battery or thermal control unit failed

P0CE0.d: P0CE0 means coolant control valve A of the battery loop is electrically sound but does not reach or hold its commanded position. GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt checks the four-port valve in stages: an end-stop learn, reaching the target within 1.5 s, drift above 3 % and a noisy feedback; 1280 of 1600 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code.
s: MIL on, often without other symptoms
Battery temperature regulation less effective
c: Control software or limits too strict (Audi, Toyota updates)
Valve sticking or actuator too weak

P0CE1.d: P0CE1 reports that coolant control valve A of the battery circuit remains in its active position although the controller commanded a change. Manufacturers phrase it differently: Mercedes hybrid battery management speaks of a shutoff valve that does not open, Volvo of a valve stuck on in the BECM of the XC90 T8 from model year 2016.
s: MIL on, usually without driving symptoms
Battery cooled or heated longer than needed
c: Monitoring limits or software too strict (Audi, Volvo updates)
Low coolant level or air in the battery coolant circuit

P0CE2.d: P0CE2 points to a ground short on the drive circuit of coolant control valve A. In the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR, GM's four-port battery valve is moved by a small motor with two driver lines.
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Valve does not move, battery thermal conditioning limited
c: Driver wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the valve connector

P0CE3.d: P0CE3 is the short-to-voltage fault of the coolant control valve A drive circuit. GM tests it on the motor-driven four-port battery valve of the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR: driver line 1 reads high while the valve should be stopped or moving forward.
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Battery heating or cooling in fallback mode
c: Driver wire pinched against a supply line
Harness damage near the battery or valve
Driver stage in the control module faulty

P0CE4.d: P0CE4 is the general circuit fault of the position feedback from the battery coolant control valve. On motor-driven valves the actuator reports its actual position as a share of the sensor supply voltage, letting the controller confirm that coolant really flows toward the battery, chiller or heater.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Valve held in a default position, thermal conditioning limited
c: Open signal, reference or ground wire of the position sensor
Damaged or corroded connector at the valve
Position sensor inside the valve actuator failed

P0CE5.d: P0CE5 means the position feedback of the battery coolant control valve is electrically valid, but the valve has not arrived where the controller sent it. In GM's 2016 Cadillac ELR tables the hybrid controller allows up to 22 s; if the feedback still shows a different position once the end-stop learn routine P1F56 has finished, 1280 of 1600 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code with the MIL on the second trip.
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Battery reaches its target temperature more slowly
c: Valve stiff from deposits or low temperature
Actuator motor weak or gearing worn
Position sensor drifted from learned end stops
Air or low coolant in the battery circuit

P0CE6.d: P0CE6 reports that the position feedback of the battery coolant control valve has fallen below its permitted window. GM expresses the signal relative to the reference voltage: the 2011 Chevrolet Volt fails it below 5 % in 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, the 2016 Cadillac ELR below 28 % in 640 of 800 samples at 6.25 ms, a value under the lowest end stop the ELR accepts during learning (just over 30 %).
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Valve position shown as near 0 % in live data
c: Feedback signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor reference voltage missing or open
Worn or defective sensor track in the actuator

P0CE7.d: P0CE7 is the high-side fault of the battery coolant control valve position feedback. GM sets it when the signal exceeds 95 % of the reference voltage in the 2011 Chevrolet Volt (40 of 50 samples at 100 ms) or 72 % in the 2016 Cadillac ELR (640 of 800 samples at 6.25 ms), in both cases with system voltage above 9 V or 10.2 V and rated Type B, so the MIL lights on the second trip.
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Valve position shown near 100 % in live data
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Worn sensor track in the actuator

P0CE8.d: P0CE8 stands for a valve position feedback that drops out or jumps briefly while the hard low and high limits are not violated long enough to set P0CE6 or P0CE7. Such patterns come from loose pins at the valve plug, a cracked solder joint or a worn sensor track that loses contact at certain angles.
s: Occasional warning lamp that may go out again
Jumping valve position in live data
c: Loose or corroded pin in the valve connector
Worn sensor track losing contact at certain positions
Cracked solder joint inside the actuator

P0CE9.d: The hybrid controller checks the control line of the electric pump that moves coolant through the power electronics loop, which in GM's Volt and ELR serves the inverter module and the high-voltage charger. GM tables from 2011 to 2016 fail it when the output driver reports an open line or a short to ground or voltage in 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid/drive system warning on
Reduced drive power because inverter and charger temperatures rise
Charging power reduced or charging interrupted
Pump not audible after switch-on when commanded via scan tool
c: Open or chafed control wire, or corroded connector at the electronics coolant pump
Failed electronics in the pump itself, drawing no current or far too much
Coolant loss from a damaged hose letting the pump run dry (Audi e-tron/Q8 e-tron bulletin)
Faulty output driver in the hybrid or thermal management control module

P0CEA.d: Here the pump circuit is electrically intact, yet the coolant it should move does not seem to arrive. GM documents it in the VICM tables of 2014 and 2016, the latter explicitly for the Cadillac ELR: with the pump enabled above 30 % speed for more than 300 s, the controller compares the power electronics coolant temperature with the temperature of the high-voltage charger.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system message
Charging slows down or stops, especially in hot weather
Reduced propulsion power during long or demanding drives
c: Air trapped in the power electronics coolant loop after service or a leak
Low coolant level in the electronics loop reservoir
Worn or partly blocked pump delivering too little flow
Skewed coolant or charger temperature signal distorting the comparison

P0CEB.d: The control line of the electronics coolant pump sits at too low a level, typically because it is shorted to ground or the driver cannot pull it up. No manufacturer publishes setting criteria for this code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid warning
Electronics coolant pump does not run
Power or charging limited as electronics temperatures rise
c: Control wire chafed through and touching body ground
Water or corrosion in the pump connector bridging pins to ground
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P0CEC.d: P0CEC flags a pump control line that is held too high, normally a short to battery voltage on the output. GM's HPC2 tables of 2016 and 2019 (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02) look for it while the pump enable is on and the commanded duty cycle is between 0 and 10 %: a line reading high when it should be nearly off counts as a failure, and 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms set the code, Type B, two trips, with system voltage above 10.2 V.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump runs permanently or does not respond to speed changes
Possible power limitation of the hybrid system
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector linking supply and control pins
Pump electronics feeding voltage back onto the control line
Output stage in the control module stuck high

P0CED.d: Some electronics coolant pumps receive two signals: a speed command and a separate enable wire that switches the pump on. P0CED concerns that enable wire.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Electronics coolant pump remains off
Reduced power or charging rate when electronics get warm
c: Broken enable wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Enable wire shorted to ground or voltage (codes it on older GM controllers)
Defective enable input inside the pump
Faulty enable driver in the control module

P0CEE.d: Sensor A reports the coolant temperature in the loop that cools the hybrid power electronics. P0CEE is the general circuit code for it, used where a controller does not tell low from high.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning
Electronics coolant pump runs continuously
Reduced drive or charging power as a precaution
c: Loose, corroded or water-soaked sensor connector
Damaged signal or ground wire of the sensor

P0CEF.d: The sensor stays electrically within range but reports a temperature that does not fit its surroundings. GM uses two kinds of comparison.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often without noticeable drivability change
Electronics coolant pump runs at odd times or longer than usual
Occasional power or charging limitation
c: Sensor element drifted and reads offset from the real coolant temperature
Added resistance from corroded terminals shifting the signal
Genuine temperature gap from poor flow or air in the electronics loop
Comparison sensor (charger, outside air or transmission fluid) reading wrong without its own code

P0CF0.d: The signal voltage of the electronics coolant temperature sensor drops close to zero, which almost always means the signal wire touches ground or the sensor is shorted internally. Low refers to the voltage, not to the temperature.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly high coolant temperature
Pump running constantly, power or charging reduced
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Water in the connector bridging signal and ground

P0CF1.d: The sensor signal rises nearly to the 5 V reference, the typical picture of an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a signal wire shorted to voltage. GM sets it above 98 % of the reference (4.9 V) in all published tables from the 2011 Volt to the 2019 HPC2 controller, 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms or 4 s within 5 s, Type B, two trips.
s: Service Hybrid Electrical System or similar warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly low coolant temperature
Charging or drive power limited
c: Water or corrosion in an underbody inline connector (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid XY291A)
Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P0CF2.d: This code catches a coolant temperature signal that jumps around faster than a liquid can actually change temperature, without necessarily leaving the valid voltage window. GM computes a string length: the controller adds up the absolute steps between four consecutive readings taken 250 ms apart.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, sometimes coming and going
Coolant temperature value jumps in live data
Pump speed or power limits change without reason
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed wire making intermittent contact with ground or another circuit
Cracked internal connection in the sensor

P0CF3.d: The control pilot is the signal line between charging station and vehicle: the station drives a 1 kHz square wave of about ±12 V, the vehicle loads it through a diode and resistors and thereby moves the level between the charging states. P0CF3 means the charge control module sees this line as interrupted, so no usable pilot reaches it although a connector is expected.
s: Charging does not start although the cable is plugged in
Charging aborts shortly after connection
Malfunction indicator lamp on and code not clearing (FCA)
c: Charging or hybrid control module software misjudging the pilot (FCA reflash bulletins)
Bent, pushed-back or corroded pilot pin in the charge inlet, or a broken pilot wire
Defective charging cable or station that delivers no pilot signal

P0CF4.d: P0CF4 flags a pilot signal that is electrically present but does not fit what the vehicle expects. GM spells out the test for the Chevrolet Volt (2011-2019, VICM/HPC2): with no cord connected and the car moving at 8 km/h or more, pilot voltage divided by battery voltage must stay below 0.03 and both processor logic states must agree; in a self-test with the internal diagnostic switch closed and the charging and venti
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
Charging refused or interrupted
Charge status indicator shows a fault
c: Faulty pilot measuring or self-test circuit inside the charging/hybrid control module
Module software needing an update (FCA Pacifica and 4xe bulletins)
Moisture or dirt in the charge inlet creating a leakage path on the pilot line
Charge door position fault blocking or distorting the test (GM Volt enable condition)

P0CF5.d: Circuit Low means the pilot level sits under the lowest value any regular charging state can produce, as happens when the pilot wire is shorted to ground or to the protective earth contact. GM checks it in the Chevrolet Volt VICM/HPC2 tables from 2012 to 2019: with the cord unplugged, the controller feeds its own test signal through the internal diagnostic switch, and the ratio of pilot voltage to 12 V battery voltag
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Station does not detect the vehicle, charging never starts
Charge status indicator shows a fault after plugging in
c: Pilot wire chafed through and touching ground or the protective earth conductor
Water or corrosion bridging pilot and earth pins in the charge inlet
Failed pilot input or test circuit in the charging control module

P0CF6.d: A pilot level above the valid range usually means the line touches a supply voltage, or the measuring path in the module reads wrongly. GM evaluates it on the Chevrolet Volt (VICM/HPC2, 2012-2019) only while no cord is connected and the car is travelling at 8 km/h or faster, a moment when the pilot should be practically dead: a normalized pilot voltage (pilot voltage over battery voltage) above 0.55, or 0.58 in the 2
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after a drive (GM Type A)
Charging does not begin at the station
Charging fault message in the cluster
c: Pilot wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness or inlet
Pilot measuring circuit in the charging control module reading too high
Moisture in a connector coupling a neighbouring voltage onto the pilot

P0CF7.d: This code stands for a pilot signal that comes and goes or jumps between levels, typically from a loose contact in the charge inlet, a plug that is not fully latched or interference on the line. Ford documents P0CF7 on the 2021-2022 Mustang Mach-E and the 2022 e-Transit, logged by the SOBDM (secondary OBD module A), and on the 2022 F-150 Lightning by the same unit, there called BCCM, the charger control module.
s: Charge status indicator flashing red (Ford)
Charging stops intermittently
Additional warning lamp with related codes such as P0A7F
c: Charger module software reacting too sensitively (Ford SOBDM/BCCM reprogramming)
Charging plug not fully seated or latched in the inlet
Worn or loose pilot contact in the inlet or on the charging cable
Charging station producing an unstable pilot signal

P0CF8.d: On the vehicle side the pilot is loaded permanently by about 2.7 kΩ, which drops the station's +12 V to roughly 9 V once a cable is connected. To ask for energy the vehicle closes charging switch A, often called S2, which adds a 1.3 kΩ branch and brings the level to about 6 V, the state in which the station closes its contactors.
s: Station detects the vehicle but charging never begins
Charging fault message after plugging in
c: Open control wire or loose connector between module and charging switch
Charging switch or its 1.3 kΩ branch open inside the module or inlet electronics
Failed driver stage in the charging control module

P0CF9.d: Charging switch A is the vehicle-side switch that adds a resistor across the pilot to tell the charging station that the car is ready to take current. P0CF9 says the effect of that switch is implausible.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Charging does not start or is refused
c: Charging switch resistor branch out of tolerance or switch with high contact resistance
Internal fault in the VICM/charging module measuring or switching circuit
Leakage on the pilot line from moisture in the charge inlet

P0CFA.d: Charging switch A shifts the control pilot from the connected state at about 9 V to the charge-request state at about 6 V by switching in an extra 1.3 kΩ path. P0CFA indicates that the control or feedback line of this switch reads too low, typically a harness wire touching ground or a driver stage in the charging module that has failed shorted.
s: Charging does not start, or starts as soon as the plug is inserted
Charging fault message in the cluster
c: Switch control or feedback wire shorted to ground
Shorted driver stage in the charging control module
Corrosion in the inlet or module connector bridging to ground

P0CFB.d: P0CFB is the high-side counterpart: the control or feedback line of charging switch A, which loads the pilot with an extra 1.3 kΩ to request charging, shows a voltage above its valid band. Typical are a short to a supply voltage in the harness or connector, or an output stage in the charging module that no longer pulls the line down.
s: Vehicle detected at the station but no energy flows
Charging cannot be stopped normally
c: Switch control or feedback wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the charging module no longer switching to ground
Lost ground at the switch letting the line float high

P0CFC.d: With P0CFC the module sees the circuit of charging switch A, which places the charge request on the pilot line, change state erratically: the signal toggles briefly or vanishes for moments, whereas lasting faults would set P0CF8, P0CFA or P0CFB. Likely triggers are a loose pin, corrosion in the charge inlet or module connector, or a chafed wire that loses contact only under vibration or temperature change.
s: Charging interrupted repeatedly, sometimes restarting by itself
Code returns after clearing
c: Loose or spread terminal in the switch circuit connector
Corrosion or moisture in the charge inlet
Chafed wire losing contact under vibration or temperature change

P0CFD.d: Stuck Off means the module commands charging switch A closed, but the pilot does not show the expected effect: the level stays at the connected value of about 9 V instead of dropping to around 6 V, so the station never receives a charge request. Possible are a switch or relay that no longer closes, an open resistor in the 1.3 kΩ branch, or a fault in the pilot measuring path.
s: Vehicle shows plugged in, but charging never begins
Charging station remains in standby or connected state
c: Charging switch or relay in the module no longer closing
Open resistor or solder joint in the 1.3 kΩ branch
Charging module software not issuing the close command correctly

P0CFE.d: Stuck On describes a charging switch A that stays closed while the module wants it open, so the pilot keeps signalling a charge request. Mercedes-Benz documents P0CFE00 in the AC charger N83, whose fault text states that the charger’s internal charge-start switch does not open.
s: Charging error message in the instrument cluster after charging
Charging aborts at home socket, wallbox or public station
Fault appears mainly with pre-entry climate control active (Mercedes-Benz)
c: On-board charger software, cured by SCN coding (Mercedes-Benz N83)
Charging switch or relay contacts sticking closed
Control line fault holding the switch permanently on

P0CFF.d: Unlike the electronics codes above, P0CFF belongs to the pump that circulates coolant through the high-voltage battery. It means the pump is commanded but does not turn, or stops.
s: Warning such as Electric drive fault or Electrical system not working correctly
Malfunction indicator lamp on (Ford)
Reduced charging speed, especially DC fast charging
Reduced drive power when the battery warms up
c: Air trapped in the battery coolant loop, pump running dry and stalling (VW ID.4, Audi Q4 e-tron)
Battery control module software misjudging pump state (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Seized or mechanically blocked battery coolant pump
Low coolant level in the battery loop
